To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccination in males, but not females, was associated with reduced innate proinflammatory cytokines and T-cell immunity and that the combination of measles and diphtheria/tetanus/pertussis vaccination was associated with reduced T-cell immunity in males but enhanced T-cell immunity in females.
DTP and MV vaccination in infants has immunological effects that may be relevant for heterologous vaccine effects.
DTP has immunosuppressive effects in males and MV has immunosuppresive effects in females, but the effects are reversed if both are given together.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immunological effects of vaccines, and in particular, the heterologous (non-targeted) effects of vaccination.
the immunological effects of vaccines and the impact these may have on the development of the immune system and the susceptibility to infection.
the heterologous immunological effects of DTP and MV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DTP vaccination in males, but not females, is associated with an attenuated innate immune response and T-cell immunity.

the results of this study indicate immunological effects of diphtheria–tetanus–acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccination on innate immunity that could account for the heterologous effect of diphtheriatetanus-whole-cell-pertussis (DwCP) vaccination on infant survival.
the effects of vaccination on the immune system are complex, and there is a need for further studies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sex-differential effects of DTP on the innate immune system are likely mediated via TLR4 and that the sex-difference in the effects of DTP is likely mediated via estrogen.
we have shown that DTP vaccination in males has a negative effect on innate immune responses and T cell immunity.

we have identified immunological effects of MV and/or DTP that could account for the heterologous protection and increased risk of death, and we have identified a sex difference in the immunological effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vaccines have effects on the immune system that can be beneficial or detrimental.
vaccines can have nontargered heterologous effects, that is, immunological effects that are unrelated to protection against the target infection.
sex is an important determinant of the immunological response to vaccines, and the sex of study subjects should be considered in vaccine trials and in the design of future studies.
